passage: Historians long treated the medieval bill of exchange as a device for sparing merchants the risk of carrying coin over dangerous roads. Yet the surviving letters between branches of the Florentine banking houses rarely mention robbery. What they discuss, at length, is the gap between the rate at which a bill was bought in Florence and the rate at which it was paid in Bruges. That gap was interest under another name, at a time when lending at interest was forbidden by the Church. The bill was less a convenience than a(n) ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The bill produced a return that was "interest under another name, at a time when lending at interest was forbidden," so its real function was to get around the ban: an *evasion*. *precaution* is the reading the first sentence sets up (protection against "dangerous roads"), and the second sentence rules it out: the letters "rarely mention robbery." *receipt* treats the bill as a mere record of payment, but the passage says the two rates differed and that the difference "was interest," so the bill earned money rather than acknowledging it. *formality* would make the rate an empty procedure, yet the letters discuss it "at length," and it carried the whole disguised return.

passage: Milestones along the Roman roads name the emperor under whom they were set up, and they were long read as a record of construction: count the stones of one reign and you have that reign's road building. But many stones stand beside roads that had been paved centuries earlier, the surfaces near them show no resurfacing of that date, and some carry the names of two or three emperors cut in succession, each new name chiselled over the last. The stones were not marking new roads. They were ______ old ones, in the name of whoever happened to rule.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The stones put the current emperor's name on roads he had not built and cut it over the names of his predecessors, so each ruler was asserting ownership of existing roads: *claiming* them. *repairing* is ruled out by "the surfaces near them show no resurfacing of that date": nothing was done to the road itself. *extending* is ruled out by "roads that had been paved centuries earlier" and by the last sentence's "old ones"; no new length was added. *commemorating* would mean honouring the roads' builders, but the names belong to "whoever happened to rule," and "each new name chiselled over the last" shows the earlier emperors being replaced, not remembered.

passage: Novels issued in monthly parts end each instalment on suspended action, and the device is usually treated as a concession to the market: the author needed readers to buy the next number. But the same authors, revising for publication in volumes when no such need remained, kept the breaks and in several cases sharpened them, and their letters discuss where a part should end in the same terms they used for where a scene should begin. For these writers the suspended ending was a matter of ______, whatever it had first been for their publishers.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The authors kept and sharpened the breaks when nothing required them and discussed their placement in the language of scene construction, so the endings were a matter of deliberate craft: *design*. *obligation* is ruled out by "revising for publication in volumes when no such need remained"; the commercial requirement had gone. *habit* would mean the breaks were retained without thought, but "in several cases sharpened them" and the letters that "discuss where a part should end" show active decision. *chance* is ruled out by the same letters: placements that are debated in advance are not accidental.

passage: The settling of English spelling in the sixteenth century is usually credited to the schoolmasters who published schemes for a rational orthography. Yet almost none of their schemes was adopted. The spellings that did become fixed are the ones found in the output of a few large printing houses, whose compositors, setting the same words thousands of times, kept whichever forms filled a line of type conveniently and dropped the rest. Standard spelling was a(n) ______ of the trade rather than of the schoolroom, and it bears the marks of the workbench, not the lecture.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Standard spelling was something the printing trade produced as it went about its work, a by-product of setting type: an *artifact* of the trade. *ideal* is ruled out by "kept whichever forms filled a line of type conveniently"; the compositors had no principle in view, and the ideals belonged to the schoolmasters whose "schemes" the passage says were not adopted. *casualty* would mean the trade damaged or destroyed standard spelling, but "the spellings that did become fixed are the ones found in the output of a few large printing houses" makes the trade its source. *ornament* is ruled out by the same convenience sentence: forms chosen to fit a line are practical, not decorative.

passage: The hallmarks struck into medieval silver are read as consumer protection: the guild guaranteed the metal so that buyers need not test it themselves. The assay records complicate this. The mark was applied only to pieces made within the town walls; imported work of equal fineness was refused it and could not then be sold legally; and the fines collected for selling unmarked silver went to the guild rather than to any buyer who had been deceived. The mark did guarantee the metal. Its purpose, though, was ______, and the buyer's confidence was a means to it.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: A mark refused to "imported work of equal fineness" and required for legal sale kept outsiders' silver off the market, so its purpose was *exclusionary*. *protective* is the reading the first sentence sets up and "the fines ... went to the guild rather than to any buyer who had been deceived" rules out: the system's rewards flowed to the guild, not to the public it supposedly shielded. *advisory* is ruled out by "could not then be sold legally"; the mark was compulsory, not guidance. *decorative* is ruled out by "The mark did guarantee the metal" and by the assay records: the stamp certified fineness rather than adorning the piece.

passage: Eighteenth-century treatises complain that singers smothered arias in ornaments the composer never wrote, and modern editions strip such ornaments away in order to recover what the composer meant. But composers' own manuscripts write out the first section of an aria in detail and leave its repeat almost bare on the page, and letters from composers to their singers ask for particular embellishments by name. Far from being the composer's intention, the bare repeat was his ______, and the singer who filled it was doing what the page asked.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: A repeat left bare by a composer who, in his letters, asks singers for specific embellishments is a space he meant them to fill: an *invitation*. *oversight* is ruled out by the contrast with the first section, which the same manuscripts "write out ... in detail"; a composer who takes that care has not forgotten the repeat. *compromise* would mean the composer yielded ornaments to singers against his wishes, but the letters "ask for particular embellishments by name." *rebuke* is ruled out by the same letters: a composer who requests ornaments is not reproaching singers for adding them.

passage: The share of brides and grooms who signed the marriage register rather than making a mark is the standard measure of literacy in early modern England. Yet reading was taught before writing, and many children left school between the two; a woman who read her prayer book fluently might still sign with a cross. Signatures therefore miss a whole class of readers. The signature rate does not overstate literacy, as critics of the measure once assumed. It ______ it, and by a margin that was larger for women than for men.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: Because people who could read but not write signed with a cross, the count of signatures falls short of the number of readers: it *understates* literacy. *inflates* is ruled out directly by "does not overstate literacy" and by the mechanism, which drops readers from the count rather than adding non-readers. *defines* is ruled out by "a woman who read her prayer book fluently might still sign with a cross": literacy is shown to exist independently of the signature. *ignores* is ruled out by the first sentence, which calls the rate "the standard measure of literacy"; a measure that captures part of the thing does not ignore it, and the last clause speaks of "a margin," which only an undercount can have.

passage: English took its words for cooked meat—beef, pork, mutton—from French while keeping native words for the living animals, and the split is taught as a snapshot of the Norman Conquest: French-speaking lords ate what English-speaking peasants raised. The earliest citations tell a slower story. For two centuries after the Conquest the French words appear only in texts written in French, and when "beef" finally enters English it names the animal as well as the meat. The pairing that seems to record a social division at a single moment was in fact ______ over generations, by speakers who had no lords to please.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The division of labour between the French and English words emerged gradually, long after the Conquest and among ordinary speakers, so it was *settled* over generations. *imposed* is the reading the first sentence sets up and is ruled out by "appear only in texts written in French" for two centuries and by "speakers who had no lords to please": no one was in a position to dictate the split, and it arrived too late to be a Conquest-era decree. *resisted* is ruled out by "when 'beef' finally enters English it names the animal as well as the meat"; the word was taken up, not held off. *forgotten* contradicts the first sentence, which shows the pairing still in use and being taught.

passage: Mining companies that paid wages in scrip redeemable only at the company store are remembered for the store's prices, and the scrip is described as a device for keeping workers in debt. Account books from several such towns show something less dramatic. Most families ended the month with a small credit, and store prices ran only a little above those in the nearest town. What the scrip prevented was not solvency but ______. A worker with a month's wages in company paper could not buy a train ticket, and the company knew it.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The sentence after the blank supplies the mechanism: scrip could not buy "a train ticket," so what it prevented was leaving, or *departure*. *saving* is ruled out by "Most families ended the month with a small credit"; families did put money by. *credit* is a trap set by that same sentence, which shows workers holding credit, not being denied it; the passage also says the debt story is "less dramatic" than remembered. *comparison* is ruled out by "store prices ran only a little above those in the nearest town": the passage itself makes the comparison and finds little in it, so hiding prices was not what the scrip achieved.

passage: Marble copies made in Roman workshops after Greek bronzes carry tree stumps and struts that the originals did not need, and the additions are usually dismissed as supports the marble required. Yet on several copies the strut is carved with as much care as the figure, and copies from one workshop show the same pose with a strut in one version and without it in another, though the block is the same stone. Buyers, it seems, wanted the strut. A stump beside the ankle told a visitor that the statue reproduced a famous bronze, and the copy's value lay in the ______.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The strut's job was to announce that the statue "reproduced a famous bronze," so what buyers paid for was the connection to the original: the *reference*. *material* is ruled out by "though the block is the same stone"; the marble did not differ between the version with a strut and the one without. *workmanship* is tempting because the strut is "carved with as much care as the figure," but the passage locates the value in what that carving "told a visitor," not in the skill of the carving itself. *pose* is ruled out by "the same pose with a strut in one version and without it in another": the pose stayed constant while the feature buyers wanted came and went.

passage: A fugitive who reached a medieval English church could claim sanctuary, and the custom is usually described as mercy: the church placed itself between a criminal and the gallows. But one coroner's rolls show that nearly every sanctuary-seeker was made to confess the crime before the coroner, to forfeit his goods to the crown, and to leave the kingdom within forty days by a road he was forbidden to stray from. For the crown this was a conviction obtained without a trial. Sanctuary was less a(n) ______ than a procedure, and the church's part in it was to supply the room.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The passage sets up the view that sanctuary spared the criminal and then shows it delivering confession, forfeiture and exile on a fixed timetable, so it was less a *reprieve* than a procedure. *punishment* fails because the passage shows sanctuary WAS punishing: "to forfeit his goods to the crown, and to leave the kingdom"; saying it was "less a punishment" contradicts that sentence. *loophole* is ruled out by "For the crown this was a conviction obtained without a trial": the arrangement served the authorities rather than letting anyone slip past them. *contest* is ruled out by "nearly every sanctuary-seeker was made to confess"; nothing was disputed.

passage: The tolls charged on eighteenth-century English canals were fixed by Parliament in each canal's founding act, and the published schedules are read as ceilings that protected traders from the canal companies. But the acts also fixed a floor: a company was forbidden to carry one merchant's coal for less than it charged another for the same cargo. The petitions asking for the floors came from the traders themselves, not from the companies, whose interest lay in the freedom to discount. What the traders feared was not high tolls but ______ ones.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The floor forbade a company "to carry one merchant's coal for less than it charged another for the same cargo," so what traders wanted prevented was a rival paying less: *unequal* tolls. *rising* is ruled out by "not high tolls" and by the ceilings the first sentence describes, which already capped increases. *hidden* is ruled out by "fixed by Parliament in each canal's founding act" and "published schedules"; the rates were public. *arbitrary* is ruled out by the same sentence: a rate set by statute is not capricious, and what the floor addressed was a lawful discount offered to one merchant and not another, which is discrimination rather than whim.

passage: The chapter headings of eighteenth-century comic novels announce the events to come—"In which our hero is robbed"—and modern readers find them clumsy, as though the author could not resist giving away his own story. But these novels were read aloud in households over many evenings, and the headings were gathered in a table of contents at the front, where a listener who had missed a night could find the place at which to rejoin. The heading was not a spoiler but a(n) ______, and its clumsiness is the clumsiness of a tool seen out of its use.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The headings let "a listener who had missed a night" locate "the place at which to rejoin," so they marked a position in the book: a *bookmark*. *preview* fails on the same sentence: the heading served someone looking back to find where the story had got to, not someone looking ahead, and a preview is exactly the spoiler the passage says it was not. *confession* takes up "could not resist giving away," but that is the modern misreading the passage rejects; nothing in the household scene involves the author owning up to anything. *joke* is tempting because the novels are comic, but the passage explains the headings by their place "in a table of contents" and their use in finding a page, not by any humour.

passage: Long runs of grain prices are the economic historian's thermometer for the pre-industrial harvest: a bad year shows as a spike. But prices were recorded at markets, and in the worst years the markets of remote districts recorded nothing at all, because no grain came in to be sold. The series that survive unbroken belong to towns able to draw grain from a distance; those towns felt the shortage, but at one remove, and their prices rose less than the empty markets' would have. The worst famines are therefore ______ in the record, precisely because they were the worst.
prompt: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
explanation: The only complete series come from towns whose prices "rose less than the empty markets' would have," so the surviving record makes the worst famines look milder than they were: *muted*. *exaggerated* is ruled out by "recorded nothing at all" and by "rose less"; the bias runs the other way. *invisible* is too strong for the passage's own account: "those towns felt the shortage" and their prices did rise, so the famine appears in the record, only softened. *delayed* has no support; the passage describes missing entries and dampened spikes, not late ones.
